about.title: Marina Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Marina residents rely on nearby Monterey County medical providers for everything from routine care to emergency treatment, and most visits end without incident. But when a provider misses a clear diagnosis, makes a surgical error, or mishandles medication, the resulting harm can upend a person's health and finances. California law treats these cases differently than ordinary injury claims: strict notice requirements, expert review, and specific damage rules all apply under MICRA. If you or a family member suspect that a bad outcome in Marina was caused by something a provider did wrong — not just an unavoidable risk — it's worth having someone look closely at the medical record and timeline. LawProactive doesn't practice law itself; we simply connect you with an independent attorney in our network who can evaluate whether your situation fits the legal definition of malpractice, free of charge and without any obligation.

whyChoose.title: Why Marina Families Turn to LawProactive

items.title: Strict Deadlines Matter
items.desc: California generally gives you one year from when you discover the harm, and no more than three years from the injury itself, to bring a claim, plus a required 90-day pre-suit notice. Missing these windows can end a case before it starts, so early guidance matters.

items.title: Expert Review Is Usually Required
items.desc: A qualified medical expert almost always has to confirm that the care fell below an accepted standard — a bad outcome by itself isn't enough. The attorneys in our network can help arrange that kind of medical review.

items.title: Understanding the Damages Cap
items.desc: California law places a cap on non-economic damages (like pain and suffering) that adjusts upward each year under MICRA. Knowing how that cap applies to your circumstances is part of building a realistic claim.

items.question: How long do I have to file a medical malpractice claim after treatment at a Marina facility?
items.answer: Generally, California law gives you one year from when you discovered (or reasonably should have discovered) the injury, and no more than three years from the date it occurred. A 90-day pre-suit notice is also required before filing. Because these timelines can be strict, it helps to get a case reviewed sooner rather than later.

items.question: Does a bad medical outcome automatically mean malpractice happened?
items.answer: No. California law requires showing that a provider's care fell below the accepted medical standard, not just that the result was disappointing or unexpected. That's why a qualified medical expert typically has to review the case before a claim can move forward.

items.question: I live in Marina but received treatment outside the city — can LawProactive still help?
items.answer: Yes. Many Marina residents receive care at facilities throughout Monterey County, and the attorney we connect you with can evaluate cases regardless of exactly which facility was involved. What matters most is reviewing the medical records and timeline of care.
